article_text:
F rantically and even stroboscopically over-energised, this big new movie from DreamWorks about best friends for ever seems to me another example of exhausting AI-type content production in animation. You could make the same argument against plenty of live-action films of course, but it is in animation that this kind of soulless blitzkrieg tends to predominate. Forgotten Island is over-controlled and over-determined, a movie that never, or hardly ever, takes its pedal from the metal, never takes a breath or a moment to let its characters come to life. At times it seems to be aping the world of Japanese anime, but without its sense of character or capacity for calm.

The story, weirdly reminiscent of The Hangover of all things, is set in the Philippines in the pre-social media 90s. Jo, voiced by R&B star HER, is a lonely and super-imaginative teen always in trouble at school; like Moana she has a wise grandma who guides her to her ancestral destiny and has captivated Jo with stories of her culture and identity – stories of the forgotten island of Nakali. Jo makes friends with similarly lonely Raissa (Liza Soberano) who like Jo is smart but with a much more focused sense of academic discipline.

Their alliance is pledged and a friendship bracelet woven, but as the years go by, poor Jo winds up with a loser’s job in a fast food joint, whereas Raissa feels guilty about leaving Jo behind as she heads for college at Caltech in the glamorous world of America. (The moment when she tells Jo she is leaving – effectively breaking up with her – is a rare moment of silence in which real emotions emerge and something is recognisably at stake.) But it is now that Jo discovers a mystical portal into the magical forgotten island of Nakali and semi-accidentally makes Raissa tumble down through this portal with her; they awaken 12 hours later to discover they have already done things here of which they have no memory and need to find out what. They also need to discover the portal which will take them back.

This Hangover-style amnesia facilitates a quest narrative, in the course of which they meet a goofy pal in the form of a wacky shapeshifting dog called Raww (Dave Franco) and a scary batibat, or memory demon, resembling Jabba the Hutt called Batiba (Jenny Slate) to whom they may have to surrender precious memories in return for freedom. They also encounter the terrifying figure of Manang (Lea Salonga) who, like Batiba may have relatable vulnerabilities that we don’t yet appreciate. And so it continues, developing and resolving with algorithmic efficiency. It leaves you with a strange sense of emptiness.

article_text:
Last night the 40th annual AFI Fest held a special screening of “Once Upon a Time…in Hollywood” at the Chinese Theatre with Quentin Tarantino in attendance. For the 900 or so Tarantino fans who packed the house, just seeing the director’s 2019 crowd-pleaser on the huge Chinese screen followed by a lively Tarantino Q&A would have been enough — but then Quentin had a surprise for the audience.

At the end of the post-screening discussion with moderator Jacqueline Coley, Coley asked Tarantino about “ The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth ,” the highly anticipated holiday release that picks up on “Once Upon a Time” stuntman Cliff’s (Brad Pitt) life in Hollywood in the 1970s. Tarantino wrote the script but isn’t directing this time out, having handed the script off to frequent Pitt collaborator David Fincher. Tarantino responded to Coley’s question about the new film with an answer that immediately sent the audience at the Chinese into a state of cinephilic ecstasy.

“I could talk a little bit about ‘The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth,'” Tarantino said. “Or…I could show you the first 17 minutes.” With that, the crowd went insane, the lights went out, and the attendees at AFI Fest got to be the first audience to get a substantive look at Tarantino and Fincher’s new opus.

Based on the footage screened, “Cliff Booth” finds Tarantino returning to his roots; like “True Romance,” “Reservoir Dogs,” and “Pulp Fiction,” it’s a crime movie heavily influenced by novelists like Elmore Leonard (who Tarantino adapted for one of his best films, “Jackie Brown”) and Raymond Chandler. It also presents a darker Cliff Booth than the one we saw in “Once Upon a Time…in Hollywood,” a version closer to the more cold-blooded, almost sociopathic Booth introduced in Tarantino’s novelization of “Once Upon a Time” than the amiable (albeit wife-murdering) fellow from the movie.

When we left Cliff Booth at the end of “Once Upon a Time…in Hollywood,” he was coming off of a sojourn in Italy to double his pal Rick Dalton (Leonardo DiCaprio); as the new film begins in June 1977, his primary connection to the film industry is a job as a projectionist at the New Beverly Cinema. (A fun in-joke that got a big laugh from the AFI Fest audience, most of whom were probably well aware that Tarantino now owns that theater.) Booth’s real profession seems to be as a kind of shady bag man and fixer, though the 17 minutes we saw at the Chinese wasn’t enough to give a strong sense of where the plot will go.

What it did give was some choice Tarantino dialogue, particularly in “Soul Brothers Die Hard,” a Blaxploitation film-within-the-film starring Yahya Abdul-Mateen II (and presumably unrelated to the 1973 movie “Brother on the Run,” which was released in some markets under the alternate title of “Soul Brothers Die Hard,” though with Tarantino you never know what kind of subterranean connection might exist). There’s also a promising relationship between Cliff and his father, a pawn shop proprietor played by Peter Weller, and enough period-accurate production design and pop culture references to assure the audience that “Cliff Booth” will be as rich in nostalgic pleasures of the late 1970s as “Once Upon a Time” was for the late 1960s.

The Q&A with Tarantino that preceded the “Cliff Booth” footage didn’t have much new information (especially for anyone who has read Jay Glennie’s doorstop of a coffee table book, “The Making of ‘Once Upon a Time…in Hollywood'”) but was fun nevertheless, thanks to Tarantino’s typical loquacity and Coley’s thoughtful line of questioning. Tarantino revealed the most personally meaningful piece of casting in a film filled with great performances — including supporting turns by multiple actors (Austin Butler, Mikey Madison, Sydney Sweeney) who have blown up in the seven years since.

“The casting that to me was the most meaningful ended up not being in the movie,” Tarantino said, recalling that Burt Reynolds was originally cast in the role of George Spahn. “He said yes, and we became friendly, but he passed away before we could make the film. But we did get to rehearse with him and do the script reading with him, so actually, the last performance Burt Reynolds ever gave was as George Spahn in the script reading.” (Bruce Dern would ultimately play the role in the finished film.)

Tarantino also referenced some of the many Easter eggs in the film, like the fact that the voice of the Pan Am flight attendant who waits on Rick Dalton on his flight back to Italy was Margot Robbie — a nod to her early work on the short-lived television series Pan Am. Tarantino also provided an extensive history of the “Canadian tuxedo” worn by Brad Pitt, a look often recognized as a tribute to Tom Laughlin in “Billy Jack.” According to Tarantino, however, the reference goes way deeper.

”It doesn’t just look like Billy Jack’s outfit; it is Billy Jack’s outfit,” Tarantino said, explaining that in the mythology he created for “Once Upon a Time…in Hollywood,” Cliff was working as a double for actor Jeff Cooper on “Born Losers,” the first film in which Tom Laughlin appeared as Billy Jack. In Tarantino’s backstory, Laughlin’s stunt double twisted his ankle, and Cliff took his place for the last week of the shoot — and for his work, he was given Billy Jack’s outfit that he wore in the movie, plus 25 bucks.

It was clear from Tarantino’s deep dive into the thinking behind elements like this costume and the set decoration in Cliff’s trailer (much of which, like many other items in the film, came from the director’s own personal collection), that behind every detail there’s a wealth of creation that never makes its way to the screen.

“The thing is, I’ve got nothing to do but invest in this mythology,” Tarantino said. “I invested in it before I did the movie, and I’ve invested in it in the years since I’ve done the movie. The audience doesn’t need to know everything. But it’s nice if I know everything.”

AFI Fest runs through Sunday night in Hollywood. “The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth” opens theatrically from Netflix on November 25.

article_text:
“ The Debut ” ended London Film Festival on a high note Sunday night as director Jesse Eisenberg and star Julianne Moore gushed over each other to a packed audience at the Royal Festival Hall.

“I mean, this movie stars my favorite person, Julianne Moore,” Eisenberg began as the duo came onstage to introduce the musical comedy. “But ironically, strangely, it’s the story of my life.”

Written and directed by Eisenberg, “The Debut” stars Moore as Mona Friedman, a shy New Jersey housewife who auditions for a part in her local theater’s production of a fictional musical called “Nosy Neighbors.” After she’s cast in the supporting role of Miss Danielle, Friedman’s life begins to unravel as she becomes more consumed with playing the part and falls under the spell of director Jerry Blankenbuehler (Paul Giamatti).

Eisenberg said he started doing community theater when he was “7 years old and miserable,” and it changed his life forever. “I wanted to write about that experience in my life, but I could only picture Julianne, to the point where I was writing it and she was inspiring me,” he added. “It’s the most thrilling experience to watch her and edit her for two years.”

Popular on Variety

Moore, wearing a chic black gown, returned the praise. She called “The Debut” an “incredible gift” and said it’s “one of the best scripts I’ve ever read in my entire life.”

“It was such an honor to receive it and such a thrill to go to work every day and to get to do this incredible part with these tremendous actors,” she said, adding of Eisenberg: “He’s a beautiful writer, exemplary director and just a great talent.”

In response, Eisenberg quipped: “I just want to note that the only time I’m called beautiful, it’s about writing.”

“The Debut” team fully leaned in for the U.K. premiere, with each guest finding a fake Playbill for “Nosy Neighbors” at their seat. During the screening, there was plenty of audible laughter and several rounds of applause for high points in Moore’s campy performance.

Ahead of “The Debut” U.K. premiere, #LondonFilmFestival attendees are given Playbills for the movie’s fictional musical “Nosy Neighbors.” pic.twitter.com/4LpSKJcaQD — Variety (@Variety) October 18, 2026

Sadly, Eisenberg said that Giamatti could not attend as he has COVID-19. “I wish he could be here. He is the greatest guy and you would love to hear him talk,” he said. “Paul’s been my favorite actor since I’m young, Julianne’s been my favorite actress since I’m young.”

Alongside Moore and Giamatti, “The Debut” also stars Eisenberg, Halle Bailey, Colton Ryan and Bonnie Milligan as actors in the musical. Bernadette Peters, Lilli Cooper, Maulik Pancholy and Havana Rose Liu round out the cast.

Of acting with his childhood heroes, Eisenberg said it was “the thrill of a lifetime” but also “very strange.”

“I was spending so much time enthralled with them, and then it was like Michael Jordan said, ‘Here, you take the ball!’ And I’m like, ‘What is this thing?’ So it was so distracting to me. I hope to never act alongside them again,” he joked. “I was my worst self.”

“The Debut” premiered at Telluride Film Festival last month, where it earned rave reviews and Oscar buzz for leading lady Moore. In Variety ‘s review , chief film critic Owen Gleiberman wrote: “‘The Debut,’ a small-town-theater comedy rooted in big ideas, is a funny and dizzying mind-bender. It’s like ‘Waiting for Guffman’ made by the Coen brothers at their most rivetingly unhinged.”

“The Debut” is set to hit theaters on Dec. 11 via A24.

Pocket Review

Bathing With the Nymphs

Olivia Zubko combines our favored legends with humankind’s most sacred pillars: beauty and bathrooms.

Hyperallergic )

Perhaps because it appeals to universal truths, we can’t seem to shake classical mythology. Humans, then and now, are freaks, drawn to stories of trickery and violence.

Not a pleasant revelation, but it may explain why Nymphaeum , Chicago-based artist Olivia Zubko’s solo show at Western Exhibitions, is so beguiling. The show combines our favored legends with humankind’s most sacred pillars: beauty and bathrooms. In this marriage, Zubko’s work is striking, pervaded by the unsettled discomfort of intimacy.

Zubko’s wall sculptures are altars to lavatories, their devotional air echoing historical nymphaeums — monuments consecrated to water nymphs. In the Hellenistic and Roman imperial periods, they were built around natural grottoes, but today, you only need to go as far as a medicine cabinet or gym to witness rituals of allurement.

article_text:
Interview

Raven Chacon Sounds the History of the Land

The Pulitzer Prize-winning Diné artist talks about his recent performances at the Park Avenue Armory, the freedom of improvisation, and the privilege of “deep listening.”

On Wednesday and Thursday night, sound mixers, synthesizers, pedals, speakers, whistles, a turkey call, and a ceramic horn sat on a table at the center of the Veterans Room in Manhattan’s Park Avenue Armory . Serving as the stage for Raven Chacon’s hour-long improvisation sessions for the Armory’s Artists Studio series, the table also offered audiences the rare opportunity to see the prolific artist at play.

During his performance on October 8, the Diné artist, composer, and Pulitzer Prize-winner used each object on the table to surprising and often discomfiting ends. He rigorously blew a whistle into a microphone, looping the sound and layering it atop a rising drone, which he intermittently cut to make room for the electronic transmission of the breath he recorded moments earlier. He mixed screeches over the whistles, eventually transforming the former into an oscillating, metallic sound redolent of the extraterrestrial signals in a sci-fi film. When the composition strayed too far into speculative abstraction, he’d snap it back with a clear, often frightening reminder of the world outside. Chacon ended the session by playing recordings of the wind through a hyperdirectional speaker that he moved in a circle around himself. He swept the sound of the wind over a new part of the room with each turn, transmitting with it the geography of alternative worlds much less violent than those sounded by the cars blaring up and down Park Avenue immediately outside, but whose continued existence depends upon our choosing to listen.

I talked with Chacon over the phone between his performances at the Armory about the role of location in his work, his repurposing of tools associated with colonial violence, and his turn to science fiction for an upcoming show at the San Francisco Museum of Modern Art .

Hyperallergic: For your Arts and Letters show, you were working with both local naturalist histories and the Lenape culture and history of New York. How do you bring site-specificity to a work like this that's entirely improvised?

Raven Chacon: I wish I could say I was responding to the Armory [ laughs ]. When I’m playing in the city, I tend to bring in more field recordings of the outdoors, of wind and other sounds from other places. A lot of these were gathered where I'm from in New Mexico. While not site-specific to the Armory in this case, I find myself incorporating those more indoors, amongst the other things that encroach upon the interior of the space. It’s unavoidable that we might hear sirens and traffic outside, and those usually become part of the soundtrack of what I’m working with.

H: Those sounds can have a different effect just based on the setting. We recently published a review of a group show you were in at the Hammer that likens your sound piece to a “ California earthquake ,” which is the type of resonance that you wouldn't get in New York.

RC: That was certainly a consideration. Also, with that show, there were a lot of works about the actual ground. That installation was situated at the entry, but immediately, you have works by Edgar Calel, Ana Mendieta, these works that involve soil and dirt. I wanted to reference that with that piece. And as you move through, you have these different interactions with different materials and visual concepts happening throughout the show.

Apartments, community centres and a pink outdoor toilet: Australia’s 2026 National Architecture award winners – in pictures

Chosen from a shortlist of more than 60 projects , the winners of this year’s Australian Institute of Architects’ annual awards were praised for their ‘architectural ambition and community benefit’

National award for urban design: Balam Balam Place, Kennedy Nolan (Victoria)

Thu 29 Oct 2026 10.00 EDT

Colorbond award for steel architecture, Sir Zelman Cowen award for public architecture and David Oppenheim award for sustainable architecture: Yitpi Yartapuultiku (The Soul of Port Adelaide), Ashley Halliday Architects, with Yitpi Yartapuultiku Aboriginal Working Group and Wax Design (SA)

National award for commercial architecture: New Sydney fish market, 3XN in association with BVN and Aspect Studios (NSW)

National award for educational architecture (joint winner): Edith Cowan University City campus, Lyons with Silver Thomas Hanley and Haworth Tompkins (WA)

National award for educational architecture (joint winner): Plant Futures Facility, m3architecture (Queensland)

National award for educational architecture (joint winner), national award for sustainable architecture (co-winner): The Forest, Woods Bagot (Tasmania)

National award for enduring architecture: Clubbe Hall, AJC Architects (NSW)

National award for heritage: Entertainment Hall White Bay, DunnHillam Architecture + Urban Design with Placemaking NSW (NSW)

National award for interior architecture: Golden Avenue, J.AR Office (Queensland)

Australian award for international architecture: Further, MORQ (Indonesia)

National award for public architecture (joint winner): Central Station, Woods Bagot in collaboration with John McAslan + Partners (NSW)

National award for public architecture (joint winner): New Footscray Hospital, Cox Architecture and Billard Leece Partnership (Victoria)

National award for residential architecture – houses (alterations and additions) (joint winner): Stuartholme House, Nielsen Jenkins with Michael Lumby (Queensland)

National award for residential architecture – houses (alterations and additions) (joint winner): Palmerston Street House, Robert Simeoni Architects (Victoria)

National award for residential architecture – houses (new): EA House, Bokey Grant (NSW)

National award for residential architecture – multiple housing (joint winner): 9 Wilson Ave, MA+Co (Victoria)

National award for residential architecture – multiple housing (joint winner): 443 Queen St, WOHA with Architectus & Kris Kowalski Architects (Queensland)

National award for residential architecture – multiple housing (joint winner): Merri Northcote, Six Degrees Architects (Victoria)

National award for small project architecture (joint winner): Magenta Outhouse, Atelier Marks Gaal (NSW)

National award for small project architecture (joint winner) and special jury prize winner: The Ablutions at Wybalenna, Taylor and Hinds Architects with the Aboriginal Land Council of Tasmania (Tasmania)

National award for sustainable architecture: Younghusband, Woods Bagot (Victoria)

Emil Sodersten award for interior architecture

article_text:
Nicholas Galitzine was grateful to shoot the “Red, White & Royal Blue” sequel after filming Peter Berg’s epic World War II drama “The Mosquito Bowl.”

“It was a slight change of pace doing that movie compared to doing this movie,” the actor told me Thursday night at “The Mosquito Bowl” world premiere during AFI Fest in Hollywood.

“Red, White & Royal Wedding,” a follow-up to the hit 2023 Prime Video romantic comedy “Red, White & Royal Blue,” sees the return of unlikely couple Prince Henry of England (Galitzine) and Alex Claremont-Diaz (Taylor Zakhar Perez), the son of the president of the United States (Uma Thurman).

Nicholas Galitzine says it was a "nice reset" working on "Red, White & Royal Wedding" after having "bombs blow up in my face for five months" while shooting "The Mosquito Bowl" pic.twitter.com/mt6aE4nE1R — Variety (@Variety) October 23, 2026

Filming wrapped in March.

“It was a nice reset going onto that film set after having bombs blow up in my face for five months,” Galitzine said.

Details about “RWRW” are being kept under wraps. Instead of following Prince Henry and Alex’s wedding, the movie reportedly features the wedding of Princess Beatrice. Prime Video has not announced a release date.

Returning cast also includes Sarah Shahi, Rachel Hilson, Clifton Collins Jr. and Stephen Fry.

“It was a really wholesome experience while adding some really amazing actors to the cast like Lena Headey,” Galitzine said. “I’m a huge fan of hers and she plays my mother in it, and so we just had a great time.”

In “The Mosquito Bowl,” Galitzine plays John McLaughry, one of four real college football stars who enlisted in the United States Marine Corps during World War II. While preparing for the Battle of Okinawa, they play in the Christmas football game Mosquito Bowl. The ensemble cast also includes Ray Nicholson as Tony Butkovich, Bill Skarsgård as George Bauman and Broadway star Tom Francis making his feature film debut as Dave Shreiner. The drama also marks sports talk show host Pat McAfee’s acting debut.

Nicholas Galitzine calls his new World War II film "The Mosquito Bowl" an "anti-war movie." #justforvariety #redcarpet pic.twitter.com/hLK5IAv2aC — Marc Malkin (@marcmalkin) October 23, 2026

The film is an emotional, terrifying and very graphic depiction of the harsh realities of war combat. “This is an anti-war movie,” Galitzine said. “It’s a representation I think of the reality of how brutal and grotesque war is. It’s also highlighting this generation that we’re all really proud of, these really young men who were just boys … We wanted to pay homage to them whilst showing the realities of war.”

The film is based on the 2022 Buzz Bissinger book “The Mosquito Bowl: A Game of Life and Death in World War II,” about the Mosquito Bowl game played during World War II.

“The Mosquito Bowl” is in theaters on Oct. 30. It premieres on Netflix on Nov. 25.

Nicholas Galitzine shows off darker hair color at "The Mosquito Bowl" premiere at AFI Fest. He told me it's for a project he starts shooting in February. #justforvariety #redcarpet pic.twitter.com/8To7jzUXWc — Marc Malkin (@marcmalkin) October 23, 2026

Galitzine also teased that his hair color on Thursday was shades darker than usual because he’s in preparation for an upcoming project. “You’ll find out soon enough,” he said, before revealing he begins shooting in February. “I’m just letting it all grow in, ya know.”

See photos from the AFI Fest world premiere of “The Mosquito Bowl” below.
